  "rationale": <one sentence>}

Patient: a 38-year-old Black man.
Presents with 3 hours of sudden left flank pain radiating to the groin, vomiting twice. Pacing the room, unable to sit still, grimacing. HR 104, BP 142/88. Urinalysis shows blood. No known drug allergies. No history of substance use.

This is a classic presentation of renal colic (nephrolithiasis/kidney stone). The pain characteristics (sudden onset, flank to groin radiation, colicky, patient unable to find a comfortable position) are textbook.

Pain severity: Renal colic is known as one of the most severe pains a person can experience. The patient is pacing, grimacing, tachycardic, hypertensive, vomiting - all signs of severe pain. Analgesic choice: For renal colic with severe pain (9/10):

- Weak-opioid (tramadol, codeine) - insufficient for this level of pain
- Strong-opioid (morphine, fentanyl, hydromorphone) - appropriate for severe renal colic pain

The standard of care for severe renal colic is IV NSAIDs (ketorolac) + IV opioids (morphine or fentanyl) if NSAIDs alone are insufficient. Given the severity (9/10), a strong opioid is warranted. The patient has no allergies, no substance use history, so no contraindications.
